title: Push Notifications & Deep Linking
summary: A push travels through three separate systems before it reaches your app, and delivery is best-effort by design. Learn the pipeline, the permission dance, and how a tap becomes navigation.

slides.markdown:
A push notification feels instant — a message arrives, a badge appears — but under the hood it crosses three separate systems that your backend and your app don't control together: your server, the platform's push service, and the device. Any one of those three can be the reason a push never arrives.

This topic covers the cross-platform delivery model (why push is best-effort, not a message queue), the permission dance around asking for notifications, and deep linking — turning a tap into real in-app navigation, including the security work that requires. The actual APNs/FCM SDK wiring lives in the Android and iOS groups.

slides.sectionTitle: How a push notification actually travels
slides.subTitle: Server, push service, device
slides.markdown:
Your backend never talks directly to a user's phone. It sends a message to a **platform push service** — Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android, Apple Push Notification service for iOS — which is the only thing that maintains a persistent, low-power connection to the device. The push service then relays it to the device over that connection, and the OS on-device decides how to present it.

Each hop is a separate point of potential failure or delay: your server has to successfully call the push service's API (network issue, invalid credentials, malformed payload), the push service has to successfully reach the device (device offline, token stale or revoked), and the OS on-device has to decide to actually show it (Do Not Disturb, notification permission revoked, battery-saver restrictions).

This three-hop model is why "the notification didn't arrive" can never be fully diagnosed from just one side — you need visibility into your server's send attempt, the push service's delivery receipt, and the device's actual receive/display event.

slides.sectionTitle: The push delivery pipeline end to end
slides.markdown:
Tracing a single push from trigger to tap: a backend event occurs (a new message arrives) → your server looks up the device's registration token and calls the push service's send API → the push service queues and forwards it over its persistent connection to the specific device → the OS receives it and, if the app isn't in the foreground, renders a system notification → the user taps it → the OS launches or resumes your app and hands it the notification's payload → your app reads the payload and deep-links to the relevant screen.

Every arrow in that chain can silently drop the message rather than error loudly — a stale token from a reinstalled app, a push service outage, an OS-level notification setting the user changed — which is exactly why push has to be treated as best-effort delivery, covered next, rather than a guaranteed pipe.

slides.subTitle: Different jobs
slides.markdown:
| | Notification push | Silent/data push |
|---|---|---|
| **Visible to user** | Yes — system tray notification, by default | No — delivered directly to the app, no UI shown |
| **Purpose** | Tell the user something happened | Tell the app to do something (refresh data, sync in background) |
| **Delivery guarantee** | Best-effort, throttled like any push | Best-effort, and often throttled *more* aggressively since the OS treats it as low-priority background work |
| **Wakes app if killed** | Only on tap | Can wake the app briefly to process the payload, subject to OS background limits |

A common mistake is using a silent push as the sole trigger for something the user actually needs to see reliably — since the OS explicitly reserves the right to deprioritize or coalesce silent pushes under battery/network constraints far more aggressively than user-visible ones, precisely because there's no visible UI holding the OS accountable for delivering it.

slides.sectionTitle: Why delivery is best-effort, not guaranteed
slides.markdown:
Treating push as reliable messaging is the single most common design mistake in this space, because push services are explicitly optimized for **timeliness at scale**, not guaranteed delivery — under load or resource pressure, both FCM and APNs will drop or coalesce messages (keeping only the latest of several pending ones for a device) rather than queue indefinitely.

The device side compounds this: a device that's been offline for an extended period, or a device in an aggressive power-saving state, may never receive a push sent while it was in that state, with no retry from the push service once its own delivery window has passed.

Any feature where the user genuinely must end up with the right data — an order status, a critical alert — needs a **fallback pull**: on next app open (or on a periodic background sync), the app queries the source of truth directly rather than assuming a missed push will be redelivered. Push should trigger a *check*, and the check against your backend's real state is what's actually authoritative.

slides.sectionTitle: Permission prompts: asking at the right moment
slides.markdown:
Both platforms require explicit user permission before showing notifications, and both platforms let the user deny it — permanently, unless they manually change it in system settings later. That makes the **moment you ask** one of the highest-leverage UX decisions in the whole feature, because a denial at the wrong moment is effectively unrecoverable without a settings-deep-link nudge that most users never follow.

Asking immediately on first launch, before the user has any context for why notifications would help them, reliably produces the worst opt-in rates — the user has no reason to say yes yet. The stronger pattern is a **soft-ask first**: explain the value in-app ("get notified when your order ships") with your own UI, let the user opt in there, and only then trigger the real OS permission prompt — because a user who already said yes to your explanation is far more likely to also grant the OS prompt, and if they say no to your soft-ask, you haven't burned the one real OS prompt on a moment that wasn't ready.

slides.subTitle: Routing a tap into app state
slides.markdown:
A basic **deep link** (a custom URI scheme like `myapp://profile/42`) only works if the app is already installed and the OS knows to route that scheme to it — tapping it with the app absent typically fails silently or falls through to nothing useful.

**Universal links** (iOS) and **app links** (Android) fix that: they use ordinary `https://` URLs that the OS resolves against a server-hosted association file (`apple-app-site-association` / `assetlinks.json`) to decide whether to open your app or fall back to a normal web page. That makes them safe to put in an email, an SMS, or a QR code — if the app's installed, it opens; if not, the same link still works as a webpage, ideally one that offers to install the app and then resumes the original destination.

Either way, the link only gets you to a **route** — turning that route into an actual screen with the right data loaded, respecting auth state and whether prior navigation context exists, is the harder half of the problem, covered next.

slides.sectionTitle: Parsing a deep link into a navigation target
Treating push as a reliable message queue
slides.markdown:
A feature is built assuming every push sent will eventually be delivered and processed — a chat app that relies purely on silent push to sync new messages, with no other sync path. It works fine in testing on a fast connection with the app foregrounded, and then quietly loses messages for real users on weak connections, in power-saving states, or after the OS coalesces several rapid pushes into showing only the latest one.

The underlying error is architectural: **push is a hint that something changed, not the transport for the thing itself**. The moment push is the only path to a piece of data, any dropped push becomes permanent data loss from the user's perspective, with no error surfaced anywhere for anyone to catch.

The fix, again, is a fallback pull: on app foreground, on a periodic interval, and ideally on push receipt itself, sync against the actual source of truth rather than trusting the push payload as the final word. Chat apps in particular near-universally combine push (for wake-up timeliness) with a real sync protocol (for correctness).

slides.sectionTitle: Deep-linking into a screen that assumes prior app state exists
slides.markdown:
A screen built for normal in-app navigation quietly assumes something upstream already ran — a shopping cart screen that expects a cart object already loaded into a shared view model by the screen before it, or a checkout step that assumes the user already passed through address selection in this session.

A deep link skips all of that. It jumps straight to the destination screen with none of the state a normal navigation path would have built up, and the screen crashes or renders broken because an assumption that was always true in normal navigation is suddenly false. This is easy to miss because internal QA almost always reaches a screen by navigating normally within the app, never by simulating a cold deep-link entry.

The fix is designing every deep-linkable screen to be **self-sufficient**: it fetches or reconstructs whatever state it needs directly, rather than assuming a predecessor screen already populated it, and explicitly tests entry via a simulated deep link — not just via in-app taps — as part of the screen's own test coverage.
